description_full: Valaris Limited, together with its subsidiaries, provides offshore contract drilling services in Brazil, the United Kingdom, Gulf of America, Australia, Angola, and internationally. It operates through four segments: Floaters, Jackups, ARO, and Other. The company owns an offshore drilling rig fleet, which includes drillships, dynamically positioned semisubmersible rigs, a moored semisubmersible rig, and jackup rigs. It also offers management services on rigs owned by third parties. The company serves international, government-owned, and independent oil and gas companies. Valaris Limited was founded in 1975 and is headquartered in Houston, Texas.

culture_narrative: Employs approximately 3K people. Revenue per employee of $623K ranks in the bottom quartile among Energy peers. Each employee generates $53K of free cash flow annually. Governance score flags low compensation governance risk (2/10).
financial_summary: Valaris Limited is a mid-cap energy business with a $5.4B market cap on $2.4B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +14% over the past three years and -5% annually across the full decade, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.
Returns on capital run at 3% against a 9% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests.

The business throws off $203M in free cash flow — roughly 9 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders. Cash conversion is thin at 0.56×, however, which raises the oldest question in analysis: are these earnings backed by cash?.
Accruals are elevated at +8.2% of assets, and Sloan showed firms building earnings through accruals rather than cash systematically underperform.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 0.8× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage runs at 5.3×.

Shareholder yield is only 1.8%, a thin return of capital, and insiders hold 12% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and within its sector the business captures 1.8× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 77%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $20.67 to $138 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.

Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 3.7% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 7.9% (vs the 8% bar).

prof: ROIC of 3% falls short of the cost of capital of 9.2%, so growth at these returns destroys value.
It converts 9% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality is a concern: cash conversion of only 0.56x and high accruals (+8.2% of assets).
ROE of 31% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.7x equity multiplier).

hlth: Leverage is conservative at 0.8x net debt to EBITDA ($599.4M of cash against $1.1B of debt), with interest covered 5.3x.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 13.9% over 3 years, 10.7% over 5 years and -5.3% over 10 years, so growth is accelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 29%).
At current returns, reinvesting 70% of profits supports about 2.1% a year of fundamental growth, too little to drive meaningful growth.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.00, a backlog worth 6% of annual revenue and deferred revenue down 5%.
Capex runs 2.3x depreciation (14.5% of sales), so it is building capacity for future growth.
Its Rule of 40 score is 18, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own 12.1%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 92%.
Shareholder yield is a modest 1.8% (1.8% in buybacks).
Short interest is elevated at 10.7% of the float, 6.7 days to cover.
people: With about 3,800 employees, each generates about $623K of revenue, 0.3x the Energy median, and revenue has grown 2.2% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $53K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $2.2M (4x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (2/10, lower is better).
